chapters.title: Chapter 6: Putting Forex Knowledge to Work

lessons.title: Red Flags: Spotting Illegal Forex Apps, Signal Groups and Ponzi Schemes

children.text: Sameer, a 31-year-old bank employee in Nagpur, is added to a WhatsApp group called "Global FX Wealth Club." The admin, who calls herself a "certified forex mentor," posts daily profit screenshots and gives free EUR/USD and gold calls that seem to work. After two weeks, she invites members to open an account on a "partner platform" and deposit through UPI. Sameer puts in ₹50,000, then ₹2 lakh more as his dashboard shows 40% gains. When he tries to withdraw, he is told to pay an 18% "tax clearance fee" first. He pays. The group goes silent. Stories like his are no longer rare: Indians reported ₹22,495 crore of cyber fraud losses in 2025, most of it in investment scams. This lesson teaches you the patterns behind forex scams, how to test any offer in minutes, and exactly what to do if you or someone you know has already paid.

body.text: Every forex scam needs three things from you: trust, urgency and a payment outside regulated channels. Refuse any one of them, by verifying registration, taking your time and paying only through verified routes, and the scam fails.

Not authorised by RBI for residents; deposits by UPI to individuals or unrelated firms

Unregistered person giving specific trade advice for money

children.text: Ponzi Maths: Why "Guaranteed" Monthly Returns Cannot Be Real

markDefs.definition: A fraud that pays earlier investors with money from newer investors, rather than from real profits, and collapses when new money slows down.

children.text: Fixed-return forex plans are almost always a

. No real trading strategy produces a guaranteed return every month, because currency markets can move against any position. A monthly promise also sounds much smaller than it really is, because it compounds.

body.caption: Converts a monthly promise into its true yearly equivalent

body.title: What "4% a month" really means
body.prompt: A "forex fund" on WhatsApp promises a guaranteed 4% return every month, compounded. What annual return is that? Round to two decimals.
body.explanation: (1.04)^12 minus 1 = 1.6010 minus 1 = 60.10% a year, guaranteed. Bank fixed deposits pay a small fraction of that, and even the best professional funds cannot promise a positive return every month. When a return is both very high and guaranteed, it is being paid from somebody else's deposit, until the new deposits stop.

body.title: The Life Cycle of a Forex Ponzi Scheme

events.title: The pitch
events.description: A charismatic "trader" or "fund" promises steady monthly returns from secret forex strategies, often with glossy offices, events or social media presence.

events.title: Early payouts
events.description: The first investors are paid on time, using money from later investors. They become the scheme's most convincing promoters.

events.title: Referral boom
events.description: Bonuses for recruiting friends and family drive rapid growth. Communities, workplaces and WhatsApp groups pile in.

events.title: Delays and excuses
events.description: Payouts slow. Investors hear about "bank issues," "market volatility" or "regulatory checks," and are offered bonuses to reinvest instead of withdrawing.

events.title: Collapse
events.description: New money dries up, withdrawals stop, the promoters disappear, and most investors lose most of their capital.

children.text: Signal Groups: How Fake Track Records Are Built

Profit screenshots prove nothing. They can come from demo accounts, be edited in seconds, or show a handful of winning trades while hiding dozens of losers. Many signal sellers earn most of their income not from trading but from subscription fees and referral commissions paid by illegal platforms for every member who deposits. A group can make money from you even if every call it gives loses.

body.title: The 64-group trick: manufacturing a perfect record

children.text: A scammer creates 64 separate Telegram groups. In week one, half get the call "buy EUR/USD" and half get "sell EUR/USD." Whichever way the market moves, 32 groups saw a winning call. The scammer deletes or ignores the losing groups and repeats the trick with the 32 winners, then 16, then 8. After a few weeks, a small number of groups have seen an unbroken streak of correct calls, purely by elimination. Those members now believe they have found a genius and happily pay for a premium subscription or deposit into the recommended app.

body.title: How many perfect records?
body.prompt: Using the 64-group trick, the scammer splits the surviving winning groups in half every week, sending opposite calls. After 6 weeks, how many groups have seen 6 correct calls in a row?
body.explanation: 64 ÷ 2 ÷ 2 ÷ 2 ÷ 2 ÷ 2 ÷ 2 = 64 ÷ 64 = 1. One group now sees a flawless six-week record that was guaranteed by design, not by skill. With 1,024 groups, 16 groups would see the same perfect streak.

body.title: A SEBI-registered adviser vs a social media tipster

columns.label: SEBI-registered investment adviser or research analyst
points: Registration number you can verify on SEBI's website
Bound by SEBI rules on disclosures, conflicts and fees
Fees collected through verified channels, such as @valid UPI handles
Grievances can be raised through SEBI's SCORES platform

columns.label: Unregistered tipster or "mentor"
points: Claims to be "certified" or "SEBI approved" without a verifiable number
No accountability if calls go wrong
Asks for payment to personal UPI IDs or unrelated accounts
Advertises accuracy rates and profit screenshots
Often paid by the platforms it pushes you towards

children.text: Follow the Money: Payment Red Flags

markDefs.definition: A bank account, often belonging to an ordinary person paid a small fee, used by fraudsters to receive and move stolen or illegal money so the real operators stay hidden.

children.text: The payment step is where most scams reveal themselves. Illegal platforms and fraud groups rarely have proper bank accounts in their own names, so they collect money through personal UPI IDs, rotating accounts of unrelated businesses, or
. Banks have flagged lakhs of such accounts to authorities. Renting out your own bank account to "help" someone receive payments can make you part of a fraud investigation.

body.label: SEBI's validated UPI handles
body.context: SEBI-registered intermediaries that collect money from investors, such as brokers, investment advisers and research analysts, use UPI IDs ending in @valid, shown with a thumbs-up icon inside a green triangle. SEBI's "SEBI Check" tool lets you verify UPI IDs and bank details. A "broker" or "adviser" asking for money on an ordinary UPI ID is a warning sign.

cells: Deposit to a personal UPI ID or a different name each time
The platform has no legitimate client money account
Dashboard shows fast, steady profits
The balance is just a number on a screen, not real money
Small withdrawal allowed early on
Bait to make you trust the platform and deposit more
Withdrawal requires paying tax, GST, fees or an upgrade first
The money is gone; each new fee is a further theft
Pressure to deposit before a "limited window" closes
Urgency to stop you from checking

body.title: Spot the safe choice
body.question: Which of these is the strongest sign that you are dealing with a legitimate, regulated entity rather than a forex scam?
options: The group admin shares daily profit screenshots from a real-looking app
The platform says it is licensed in a foreign country and has a slick website
The broker is SEBI-registered, trades are on NSE or BSE, and payments go to a verified @valid UPI handle
Hundreds of members in the group say they made money
body.explanation: Verifiable SEBI registration, exchange-traded contracts and verified payment channels can all be checked independently. Screenshots, foreign licences for dealing with Indians, and testimonials in a group controlled by the promoter can all be faked or planted.

body.text: After a loss, expect a second wave. Recovery scammers find victims through complaint forums and the same groups, posing as lawyers, cyber cells, ED officers or "fund tracing agencies," and ask for an upfront fee to get money back. Genuine police, courts and regulators do not charge victims to pursue a case. Anyone promising guaranteed recovery for a fee is running another scam.

children.text: If You Have Already Paid: What to Do, Fast

body.title: Immediate steps after a forex or investment fraud
steps: Stop all further payments, including any "fees" to unlock withdrawals.
Call the national cyber fraud helpline 1930 as soon as possible; speed improves the chance of freezing the money trail.
File a complaint on cybercrime.gov.in with transaction IDs, UPI IDs, bank details, app names and screenshots.
Inform your bank immediately and ask it to report and dispute the transactions.
Preserve all chats, emails, app screenshots and payment records; do not delete the group or the app.
Report unauthorised deposit-taking schemes on RBI's Sachet portal.
Ignore anyone offering paid recovery services, and consult a lawyer if you are unsure about your own legal position.

body.label: National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal
body.description: The Government of India portal for reporting online financial fraud. For urgent cases, call the 1930 helpline.

body.label: RBI Sachet Portal
body.description: Check whether an entity is registered with a financial regulator and report unauthorised schemes that collect money from the public.

body.title: Diagnosing Sameer's scam
body.scenario: Go back to Sameer's story from the start of this lesson: the WhatsApp group, the "certified mentor," free calls that seemed accurate, the partner platform, UPI deposits of ₹2.5 lakh, a dashboard showing 40% gains, and an 18% "tax clearance fee" to withdraw. Sameer has now paid the fee, and the group has gone silent. A new contact messages him saying they are from a "cyber recovery agency" and can get his money back for ₹25,000.
body.prompt: Identify every red flag in Sameer's journey, name the type of scam, explain why the "gains" were never real, and list what Sameer should do now, including how to respond to the recovery offer.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Red flags: being added to an unknown investment group; a "certified mentor" with no verifiable SEBI registration; free calls used to build trust, possibly through the group-splitting trick; a "partner platform" rather than a SEBI-registered broker on NSE or BSE; deposits by UPI to non-verified IDs; unusually fast, steady profits; and a fee demanded before withdrawal.
2. Scam type: a fake platform and investment group scam, combined with an unauthorised forex and gold trading offer. The mentor likely earned money from every deposit.
3. The gains were never real. The dashboard was a number controlled by the platform. The money was probably moved out through mule accounts soon after each deposit, and the 18% "tax" was simply a further theft, since genuine taxes are not paid to a trading app before withdrawal.
4. What to do now: stop all payments; call 1930 immediately and file a complaint on cybercrime.gov.in with every UPI ID, transaction reference and screenshot; ask his bank to report and dispute the transactions; keep all chats and app records; and report the scheme through RBI's Sachet portal.
5. The recovery offer is a second scam. Genuine authorities do not charge victims. He should not pay, should add the contact's details to his cybercrime complaint, and warn others in his circle about the group.

body.title: The emergency number
body.textWithBlank: If you are a victim of online financial fraud in India, call the national cyber fraud helpline number ___ immediately.
body.explanation: The 1930 helpline is run under the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre. Reporting quickly gives banks and police the best chance of freezing money before it is moved through mule accounts.

cards.definition: Pays old investors with new investors' money and collapses when new deposits slow. Usually promises steady guaranteed returns.
Sending opposite calls to different groups so some always see a perfect record by chance.
A bank account used by fraudsters to receive and move illegal money while hiding the real operators.
SEBI's verified UPI ID format for registered intermediaries, in use from 1 October 2025.
A demand for tax, GST or fees before withdrawing. A sign the balance was never real.
A follow-up fraud offering to recover lost money for an upfront fee, often posing as lawyers, police or agencies.

points: Indians reported ₹22,495 crore of cyber fraud losses in 2025, with investment scams making up about three-quarters.
Forex scams take five common forms: offshore leveraged apps, signal and mentor groups, fixed-return Ponzi plans, fake platforms built on trust, and recovery scams.
Guaranteed monthly returns compound into impossible annual figures: 4% a month is about 60% a year.
Profit screenshots and perfect track records can be faked or manufactured by splitting groups and hiding losers.
Payment is the giveaway: verify SEBI registration, use exchange-traded contracts, and pay only through verified channels such as @valid UPI handles.
If you have paid, stop further payments, call 1930, file on cybercrime.gov.in, alert your bank, preserve evidence, and ignore paid recovery offers.

body.text: This lesson is for education and awareness only and is not legal advice. Fraud statistics are based on government data reported in the media and may be revised. Scam patterns change quickly. If you believe you have been defrauded, report it immediately through official channels and consult a qualified lawyer about your specific situation.
